items.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002
items.q: invited me over and listened to the album, and was just beautiful about it.

ctx.x: Oh yeah. I mean I think most musicians start off being mostly affected by people on their instrument and then they expand their auditory interests. For me the very first jazz piano album I can recall hearing was an album my piano teacher brought me, it was a ten inch MGM LP called “You’re Hearing George Shearing.” And I remember hearing that album and saying woo, who is this guy? Listen to that marvelous classical technique and yet there’s this wonderful rhythmic thing going and he’s improvising, and I want to…

on the near west side. And again, because I was tall I could get in there, and I remember just spending nights listening to the Billy Taylor Trio and it just was wonderful music. Then I got a chance to hear Oscar Peterson at the London House in Chicago, which used to be a wonderful supper club. And I remember not only being knocked out by Oscar but even more so by Ray Brown, just the force and the drive of that playing, and I was thinking gee I hope someday I can play with a bass player like that. So I would say…

invited me over and listened to the album, and was just beautiful about it. I mean Bill was always so comfortable with his own playing, I mean even though he was very self- critical, but he knew his playing. So he didn’t have to be competitive with anybody, he didn’t have to get into putting people down or anything. So he just encouraged me to do my thing. He said, “look I don’t have anything to suggest except play your music. You’re doing it. Just keep doing your music.” And that was a tremendous encouragement…
